items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Oregon’s Painted Hills are rounded clay hills marked by distinctive red, yellow, tan, and black bands.
• The bands began as volcanic ash deposited by eruptions about 30 to 40 million years ago.
• Each ash layer gradually weathered into soil before subsequent eruptions buried it.
• The minerals that formed in each soil depended on the prevailing climate.
• Warm, humid conditions produced iron-rich red soils, while cooler, drier conditions produced yellowish and tan soils.
items.stem: The student wants to explain why the bands of the Painted Hills differ in color. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Because each band began as ash from a different volcanic eruption, the bands of the Painted Hills contain different minerals and therefore show different colors.
The red bands of the Painted Hills formed during cooler, drier periods, whereas the yellowish and tan bands formed when the climate was warm and humid.
Each band of the Painted Hills is a former soil that developed from ash under a particular climate, which determined the band’s minerals and thus its color.
Deposited by eruptions about 30 to 40 million years ago, the volcanic ash in the Painted Hills gradually weathered into soil, layer by layer.
items.explanation: The goal is to explain why the bands differ in color. The notes link three facts: each ash layer “gradually weathered into soil,” the minerals in each soil “depended on the prevailing climate,” and those minerals set the color (“Warm, humid conditions produced iron-rich red soils, while cooler, drier conditions produced yellowish and tan soils”). Choice C joins them: each band formed under its own climate, which fixed its minerals and so its color.

A.why_wrong: It gives a reason for the colors, but the notes tie each soil’s minerals to the prevailing climate, not to which eruption produced the ash.

B.why_wrong: It links color to climate but reverses the notes: red soils formed in warm, humid conditions, and yellowish and tan soils in cooler, drier ones.

D.recipe: PART (how the layers formed, not why they differ)
D.why_wrong: It explains how the ash became layers of soil, but it never mentions climate or minerals, so it does not explain why the bands differ in color.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (geology of the Painted Hills, John Day Fossil Beds, Oregon). Real subject known without a search; no named people (WAVE.md: no fact-checking for this skill). Option fact check: A FALSE goal-shaped (eruption instead of climate), B FALSE goal-shaped (climates reversed), D true but partial. Goal-only solve (without the notes): A, B and C all explain the colors.
band7_moves: why-goal over a three-bullet chain (ash weathered into soil, climate set the minerals, minerals set the color)
key states the derived link (climate determined minerals and thus color) in words the notes do not use
two goal-shaped FALSE options: a wrong cause (separate eruptions) and the climates reversed
one accurate partial option (how the layers formed)

band7.why: Why-goal over a three-bullet chain (ash to soil, climate to minerals, minerals to color), as ee51ad04; key states the derived link in its own words; two goal-shaped FALSE options (separate eruptions as the cause, climates reversed) and one true PART; a goal-only solve leaves A, B and C. Notes 27% rare words, 5.44 chars per word.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Buried stone structures absorb and release heat differently than the surrounding soil.
• After sunset, such structures often stay slightly warmer than the surrounding ground.
• A team of archaeologists wanted to map a buried ancestral Puebloan village in New Mexico without excavating it.
• Before dawn, they flew a drone equipped with a thermal camera, which detects temperature differences, over the site.
• The resulting images revealed outlines of walls and rooms that were invisible at the surface.
items.stem: The student wants to present the study’s aim and methodology. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Hoping to map a buried village in New Mexico without excavation, archaeologists flew a drone equipped with a thermal camera over the site before dawn.
Thermal images taken by a drone over a buried village in New Mexico revealed outlines of walls and rooms that were invisible at the surface.
Because buried stone structures absorb and release heat differently than soil, they often remain slightly warmer than the surrounding ground after sunset.
Archaeologists studying a buried ancestral Puebloan village in New Mexico wanted to map its layout without excavating the site.
items.explanation: The goal has two parts: the aim (what the team wanted to do) and the methodology (how they did it). Choice A gives both: the archaeologists “wanted to map a buried ancestral Puebloan village in New Mexico without excavating it,” and they “flew a drone equipped with a thermal camera” over the site “Before dawn.”

B.why_wrong: It mentions the drone’s thermal images but reports what they revealed, a finding, and never states what the archaeologists set out to do.

C.why_wrong: It explains why buried structures stay warmer than the surrounding ground after sunset, the idea behind the method, but it mentions neither the study’s aim nor how the team carried it out.

D.why_wrong: It states the aim but says nothing about the drone or the thermal camera, so the methodology is missing.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (thermal imaging of a buried village from a drone). Real technique, described generically; the team is unnamed and no figures are given (WAVE.md). Band 6 shape: study-slot distractors (finding, principle, aim only).

fixes: notes bullet 2: “warmer than the ground above them” to “warmer than the surrounding ground”, so the accurate background option C matches the notes

band7.why: Planned band 6: aim and methodology with study-slot distractors (method plus finding, background principle, aim only), the band-6 STUDY shape of 8d1ddd1b. Notes 16% rare words, 5.39 chars per word.

items.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Fleets from Europe and North America fished for cod on the Grand Banks, off Newfoundland, for nearly five centuries.
• Beginning in the 1950s, industrial trawlers dragged enormous nets across the banks and froze their catch onboard.
• Catches soared for two decades, but fish were being caught faster than they could reproduce.
• In 1992, with the northern cod stock near collapse, Canada imposed a moratorium on commercial fishing.
• The moratorium eliminated tens of thousands of jobs, and the stock has recovered only partially since.
items.stem: The student wants to provide an overview of the history of the Grand Banks cod fishery. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: For nearly five centuries, industrial trawlers caught Grand Banks cod faster than the fish could reproduce, until Canada imposed a moratorium in 1992 from which the stock has only partially recovered.
Canada’s 1992 moratorium on commercial fishing, which eliminated tens of thousands of jobs, pushed the Grand Banks cod stock to near collapse after five centuries of fishing.
Beginning in the 1950s, industrial trawlers that froze their catch onboard enabled fleets to catch cod on the Grand Banks faster than the fish could reproduce.
Fished for centuries, the Grand Banks cod were driven to the brink of collapse by decades of industrial trawling; Canada halted commercial fishing in 1992, but the stock has never fully recovered.
items.explanation: An overview has to span the whole history: centuries of fishing, the trawler era, the near collapse and the 1992 moratorium, and the slow recovery. Choice D covers every stage and gets each link right: cod were fished for “nearly five centuries,” industrial trawlers arriving “Beginning in the 1950s” caught fish “faster than they could reproduce,” the stock fell “near collapse,” Canada “imposed a moratorium on commercial fishing,” and the stock “has recovered only partially since.”

A.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped: trawling stretched over five centuries)
A.why_wrong: It spans the whole history, but it gives the five centuries of fishing to industrial trawlers; the notes say the trawlers arrived only “Beginning in the 1950s,” after nearly five centuries of fishing by earlier fleets.

B.why_wrong: It spans the history but reverses cause and effect: the stock was already near collapse when Canada imposed the moratorium, so the moratorium did not push it there.

C.why_wrong: It describes only the trawler era and why catches outpaced reproduction; the long history before it, the moratorium and its aftermath are missing.

items.notes: Subject: history and environmental science (collapse of the northern cod fishery). Real event known without a search; figures kept general (five centuries, tens of thousands of jobs); no named people. Option fact check (after review): A FALSE goal-shaped (industrial trawling dated to the whole five centuries), B FALSE goal-shaped (moratorium caused the collapse), C true but one stage. Goal-only solve: A, B and D all read as overviews.
band7_moves: overview over a five-bullet arc (long fishing history, trawlers, overfishing, moratorium, partial recovery)
key paraphrased away from the notes (brink of collapse, halted commercial fishing, never fully recovered)
two goal-shaped FALSE options that span the arc with one wrong link: five centuries of industrial trawling, and the moratorium as the cause of the collapse
one accurate partial option (the trawler stage only)

fixes: A rewritten: was “rebounded quickly”, killed by one glance at the last bullet; now a full-arc overview that dates industrial trawling to the whole five centuries (bullet 2 says 1950s)
key D paraphrased away from the notes (was “near collapse ... 1992 moratorium ... recovered only partially”)
explanation and A why_wrong rewritten, quotes checked word for word

band7.why: After the A rewrite and key paraphrase: two goal-shaped FALSE overviews each with one wrong link (five centuries of trawling; moratorium as cause of the collapse), one true PART; key no longer echoes the notes. Stronger than 964c6055, which has no FALSE option. Notes 21% rare words, 5.21 chars per word.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Varves are annual pairs of sediment layers that accumulate on the beds of certain lakes.
• Each pair consists of a pale, coarse layer deposited in spring and summer and a thin, dark layer deposited in winter.
• Researchers examined varves spanning approximately 2,000 years in a lake in northern Sweden.
• They discovered that the pale layers were thickest in years with substantial spring snowmelt.
• Vigorous meltwater transports additional sand and silt into the lake.
items.stem: The student wants to present the study’s findings to an audience already familiar with varves. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Examining varves, the yearly pairs of pale and dark sediment layers that accumulate in certain lakes, researchers in northern Sweden discovered that the pale layers were thickest in years of heavy spring snowmelt.
Researchers studying roughly 2,000 years of varves in a lake in northern Sweden discovered that the pale layers were thickest in years of heavy spring snowmelt.
Researchers examined varves spanning approximately 2,000 years of sediment in a lake in northern Sweden.
Researchers studying varves in a lake in northern Sweden discovered that the dark winter layers were thickest in years of heavy spring snowmelt.
items.explanation: The audience already knows what varves are, so the sentence should use the term without defining it and report what the researchers found. Choice B does this: it names the study and gives the finding that “the pale layers were thickest in years with substantial spring snowmelt.”

A.why_wrong: It reports the finding correctly but stops to explain what varves are, which this audience already knows.

C.why_wrong: It says what the researchers examined but gives no finding.

D.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped: finding attached to the wrong layer)
D.why_wrong: It presents a finding without re-defining varves, but the notes say the pale layers, not the dark winter layers, were thickest in years of substantial snowmelt.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (lake varves and snowmelt). Varves are real; the study is generic and unnamed, with no invented figures beyond the span of the record (WAVE.md). Written as a strong band 6: AUD_FAM has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/rhetorical_synthesis.md), so band_target is 6 though the plan cell said 7. Option check: A complete but re-defines varves (the 2.1 D trap), C partial, D FALSE goal-shaped.

band7.why: AUD_FAM has no band-7 official items (spec/rw/band7/rhetorical_synthesis.md), so it cannot be band 7; the writer rightly set band_target 6. Strong band 6 on 39ccb463 and 2.1: a complete option that fails only by redefining varves, a goal-shaped FALSE (wrong layer) and a PART. Notes 23% rare words.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Salt glazing gives stoneware a glassy surface during firing rather than beforehand.
• Potters stack unglazed vessels inside a kiln and heat them to about 1,200°C.
• At that temperature, they introduce ordinary salt through small openings in the kiln’s walls.
• The salt vaporizes, and sodium from the vapor combines with silica in the clay’s surface.
• This reaction produces a thin glassy coating, frequently with a pitted texture resembling orange peel.
items.stem: The student wants to describe how a salt glaze forms on a pot. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Potters heat unglazed vessels to about 1,200°C and then add ordinary salt to the kiln, where the salt melts and spreads over the clay to form a thin glassy coating.
When salt is introduced into a kiln heated to about 1,200°C, silica from the salt vapor combines with sodium in the clay to form a thin glassy coating.
Salt introduced into a kiln at about 1,200°C turns to vapor, and its sodium bonds with silica on the vessels’ surfaces, producing a thin glassy coating.
Salt-glazed stoneware is fired at about 1,200°C and frequently has a thin glassy coating with a pitted texture that resembles orange peel.
items.explanation: The goal is to describe how the glaze forms, so the sentence must follow the process in the notes: salt is added to the hot kiln, “The salt vaporizes, and sodium from the vapor combines with silica in the clay’s surface,” producing the glassy coating. Choice C traces those steps with each substance in its right role.

A.why_wrong: It gets the order of steps right, but the notes say “The salt vaporizes, and sodium from the vapor combines with silica in the clay’s surface”; the salt does not melt and spread over the clay.

B.why_wrong: It follows the right steps but swaps the substances: the sodium comes from the salt vapor and the silica from the clay.

D.why_wrong: It gives the firing temperature and what the finished coating looks like, but it never says what the salt does, so it does not describe how the glaze forms.

items.notes: Subject: arts and technology (salt-glazed stoneware). Real technique known without a search; no named people. The process is given in plain ordered bullets, without “Step” labels (only one official item uses them). Option fact check: A FALSE goal-shaped (after review: salt melts and spreads instead of vaporizing and reacting), B FALSE goal-shaped (sodium and silica swapped), D true but off goal. Goal-only solve: A, B and C all describe a process.
band7_moves: process description traced across three ordered bullets (salt added in the kiln, vaporizes, sodium joins silica)
two goal-shaped FALSE options that each garble one step: the salt melting and spreading instead of vaporizing and reacting, and the two substances swapped
one accurate off-goal option (what the finished glaze looks like)

fixes: A rewritten: carried two errors (salt coated on before firing, salt melts), the first killed by bullet 1; now right timing with one mechanism error (melts and spreads, against bullet 4)

band7.why: After the A rewrite: as b07a7634, each FALSE option garbles one step of the process (melts instead of vaporizing and reacting; sodium and silica swapped), so the student must trace bullets 2 to 4; D is a true off-goal option. Notes 32% rare words, 5.29 chars per word.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Shotgun houses and dogtrot houses are two traditional styles of home once common throughout the southern United States.
• A shotgun house is a single room wide, with its rooms arranged one directly behind another.
• Its front and back doors typically align, allowing air to pass straight through.
• A dogtrot house consists of two rooms or cabins on either side of an open, roofed passageway.
• This central passageway, called the dogtrot, channels breezes that help cool the house.
items.stem: The student wants to contrast how rooms are arranged in the two styles of house. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Both shotgun houses and dogtrot houses were designed so that air could move through them and help cool the rooms.
Whereas a shotgun house’s rooms are lined up one behind another, a dogtrot house’s rooms sit on either side of an open central passageway.
A dogtrot house has two rooms or cabins on either side of a roofed passageway known as the dogtrot.
Shotgun houses and dogtrot houses, two styles of home that were once common across the southern United States, arrange their rooms in very different ways.
items.explanation: The goal is to contrast the room arrangements. Choice B sets them side by side: in a shotgun house the rooms are “arranged one directly behind another,” while a dogtrot house has rooms “on either side of an open, roofed passageway.”

A.why_wrong: It states something the two styles share, letting air move through to cool the house, rather than contrasting how their rooms are arranged.

C.why_wrong: It describes only the dogtrot house; the shotgun house is not mentioned, so there is no contrast.

D.why_wrong: It says the two styles arrange their rooms differently but never says how either one does.

items.notes: Subject: arts and architecture (vernacular houses of the US South). Real house types known without a search; no named people (WAVE.md). One shared trait (airflow) feeds the REL option; one differing attribute (room layout) is the goal.

review.note: Kept per caller: different subject from the Words in Context Project Row Houses item.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Written Chinese uses characters, and each one usually stands for a single syllable.
• In the 1950s and 1960s, mainland China introduced simplified characters to help more people learn to read and write.
• Many simplified characters have fewer strokes than the older, traditional forms.
• Simplified characters are now standard in mainland China and Singapore.
• Traditional characters are still standard in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macau.
items.stem: The student wants to contrast where simplified and traditional characters are used. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Mainland China introduced simplified characters in the 1950s and 1960s to help more people learn to read and write.
Written Chinese uses characters, which usually stand for single syllables and can be written in either simplified or traditional form.
Many simplified characters have fewer strokes than the traditional forms they replaced.
Simplified characters are standard in mainland China and Singapore, whereas traditional characters are still the norm in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macau.
items.explanation: The goal is to contrast where each form is used. Choice D does so: simplified characters are “standard in mainland China and Singapore,” while traditional characters “are still standard in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macau.”

A.why_wrong: It gives the origin and purpose of simplified characters only and says nothing about where either form is used.

B.why_wrong: It explains what Chinese characters are and that two forms exist, but it does not say where either form is used.

C.why_wrong: It contrasts the two forms by number of strokes, not by where they are used.

items.notes: Subject: social science and language (simplified and traditional Chinese characters). Real, well-established facts known without a search; no named people.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• The kayak was a narrow, enclosed boat usually paddled by a single hunter.
• Its covered deck kept out icy water as the hunter pursued seals and other animals.

items.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference between the kayak and the umiak. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: While the kayak usually carried a lone hunter, the umiak could carry an entire family and its belongings.
Both the kayak and the umiak were made by stretching animal skins over a frame of driftwood or bone.
With its covered deck keeping out icy water, the narrow kayak allowed a single hunter to pursue seals and other animals.
Inuit and Yupik peoples of the Arctic traditionally built two kinds of boats that differed in important ways.
items.explanation: Choice A contrasts the two boats on one attribute, their size and who they carried: the kayak was “usually paddled by a single hunter,” whereas the umiak “could transport an entire family and its belongings.”

B.why_wrong: It states what the two boats have in common, how they were built, rather than a difference between them.

C.why_wrong: It describes only the kayak; the umiak is not mentioned.

D.why_wrong: It says the two kinds of boats differed without saying how.

items.notes: Subject: history and culture (Arctic skin boats). Real boat types known without a search; no named people. Only the key states any difference, so no second option meets the goal.

Bangladeshi American structural engineer Fazlur Rahman Khan developed tube systems that allowed skyscrapers to rise higher while using less steel.
Designed with a system created by Bangladeshi American structural engineer Fazlur Rahman Khan, Chicago’s Willis Tower consists of nine square tubes of varying heights joined together.
In a tube system, most of the wind’s force is resisted by a building’s exterior walls rather than by its interior columns.
items.explanation: The sentence must describe the tower’s structure and tell an unfamiliar reader who Khan is. Choice C identifies him as a “Bangladeshi American structural engineer” and describes the tower: “nine square tubes of varying heights joined together.”

A.why_wrong: It describes the structure but refers to “Khan” without saying who he is, which an unfamiliar audience would need.

B.recipe: OG (introduces the engineer, not the tower)
B.why_wrong: It identifies Khan and his tube systems but never describes the Willis Tower.

D.why_wrong: It explains how tube systems handle wind but mentions neither the Willis Tower nor Khan.

items.notes: Subject: history and technology (Fazlur Rahman Khan, bundled tube, Willis Tower, formerly Sears Tower). Real person and facts known without a search (WAVE.md: real subjects known well are welcome).

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Karesansui, or “dry landscape,” is a style of Japanese garden that contains no water.
• Its designers arrange rocks to suggest mountains or islands and rake gravel into patterns that suggest flowing water.
• Many such gardens were created at Zen Buddhist temples beginning in the 1300s.
• In 1939, designer Mirei Shigemori created four gardens around the abbot’s hall at Kyoto’s Tōfuku-ji temple.
• One of them arranges square stones and moss in a checkerboard pattern.
items.stem: The student wants to introduce karesansui to a new audience. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: A style of Japanese garden that contains no water, karesansui uses rocks to evoke mountains or islands and raked gravel to evoke flowing water.
Mirei Shigemori’s karesansui gardens at Kyoto’s Tōfuku-ji temple, created in 1939, include one that arranges square stones and moss in a checkerboard pattern.
In 1939, designer Mirei Shigemori created four gardens around the abbot’s hall at Tōfuku-ji, a temple in Kyoto, Japan.
Beginning in the 1300s, many karesansui gardens were created at Zen Buddhist temples.
items.explanation: A new audience needs to learn what karesansui is. Choice A says it is “a style of Japanese garden that contains no water” and explains how its rocks and raked gravel stand for mountains, islands and water.

B.why_wrong: It describes one karesansui garden but uses the term without explaining it, so a new audience would not learn what karesansui is.

C.why_wrong: It reports when and where Shigemori made four gardens; it does not mention karesansui or say what it is.

D.why_wrong: It gives when and where such gardens were made but never says what karesansui is.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Japanese dry landscape gardens; Mirei Shigemori’s 1939 gardens at Tofuku-ji, including the checkerboard moss garden). Real subject known without a search.

Survey teams measured long chains of triangles across India with heavy instruments called theodolites.
Surveyor William Lambton began the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India in 1802.
Expected to take about five years, the Great Trigonometrical Survey of India lasted nearly seven decades, from 1802 until 1871.

B.why_wrong: It describes how the teams measured the land, not how long the work lasted.
